claims.text: Historically, Indian textile production was acclaimed worldwide for applying natural dyes to cotton, a difficult fibre to dye, and for the vivid, fast colours that resulted.

quotes.quote: Historically, Indian textile production has been acclaimed worldwide for the alchemy of applying natural dyes to cotton fabric-a difficult fiber to dye-and for the resulting vivid and fast colors.

claims.text: Both in the past and today, Indian artisans have been known for skilful and ingenious use of local materials to produce exquisite textiles.

quotes.quote: Both in the past and up to the present day, Indian artisans have been known for their skillful and ingenious use of local materials to produce exquisite textiles.

claims.text: Ornamentation is a key aspect of craftsmanship in the Indian subcontinent, and it is perhaps most striking in the region's textile crafts.

quotes.quote: Ornamentation has been a key aspect in the long history of craftsmanship in the Indian subcontinent - and this is perhaps most striking in the region's textile crafts.

claims.text: The specialised skills of embroidery, sometimes months of work on a single garment, often make embroidered textiles luxury goods.

quotes.quote: The specialised skills and techniques of embroidery that artisans use - sometimes spending months at a stretch on a single garment - often make for luxury textiles.

claims.text: Indian applique traditions such as pipili, tharu, kantha and khatwa repurpose fabric from old or damaged garments into everyday items such as bags and quilts, including the kowdhi.

quotes.quote: Appliqué traditions such as pipili, tharu, kantha, and khatwa repurpose fabric from old or damaged garments to make everyday items that include quilts, such as the kowdhi, and bags.
There are several applique traditions in India, most traditionally used as a means to recycle leftover fabric.

claims.text: Some Indian embroidery techniques, such as beetle wing and sozni embroidery, are complex enough to have resisted mechanisation.

quotes.quote: Many of these techniques are complex enough to have resisted mechanisation, such as those of beetle wing and sozni embroidery.

claims.text: Notable types of carpets and rugs from across India include gabba, kaleen, galeecha and dhurrie.

quotes.quote: Notable types of carpets and rugs from across India include gabba, kaleen, galeecha and dhurrie.

claims.text: Dhurries are distinguished from carpets by their flat weave, their relative lightness and their often reversible designs.

quotes.quote: Dhurries are distinguished from carpets by their flat weave, their relative lightness and their often-reversible designs.

claims.text: Rajasthan, with its neighbouring state of Gujarat, has a long-established tradition of resist-dyed textiles, particularly bandhani.

quotes.quote: Rajasthan, along with its neighbouring state of Gujarat, has a long-established tradition of resist-dyed textiles, particularly the technique of bandhani.

claims.text: As India pursued rapid industrialisation from the 1950s, traditional clients came to prefer cheaper mass-produced textiles and artisans were forced towards distant urban markets.

quotes.quote: In the 1950s, as India began nation building, the government focused on rapid industrialization.

With the influx of industrially produced goods, traditional clients began to prefer cheaper, newly available mass-produced textiles over handcraft, and artisans were forced to look to distant, unknown markets in urban centers.

claims.text: Khatri dyers of Kutch historically bartered their dyed fabrics directly to their users for milk, animals and grain.

quotes.quote: They bartered their dyed fabrics directly to their users for milk, animals, and grain.

claims.text: At Sanganer, laborious hand block printing gave way in the 1960s to screen printing, which used synthetic dyes and chemicals for bleaching.

quotes.quote: This laborious process gave way to screen printing in the 1960s, which tried to piggy back on the reputation of block printing. Screen printing was a cost effective, mechanical and faster way of printing by using synthetic dyes and chemicals for bleaching.

claims.text: Dabu's naturally derived indigo, yellow and red have given way to synthetic products such as Naphthol for red, with tar replacing the mud resist.

quotes.quote: the colours - indigo, yellow and red - were naturally derived but have given way to synthetic chemical products such as Naphthol for red colour and tar instead of the mud-resist

claims.text: Cotton is a seed-hair fibre from plants of the genus Gossypium.

quotes.quote: Extracted from the cotton plants of the genus Gossypium, cotton is a seed-hair fibre used to make fabric.
A strong, natural vegetable fiber obtained from the exterior of the seeds of various species of Gossypium native to India, the Sudan, and Ethiopia.

claims.text: Cotton contains 88-96% pure alpha cellulose, the remainder being protein, pectin, sugar, oil and wax.

quotes.quote: It contains 88-96% pure alpha cellulose; the remainder is protein, pectin, sugar, oil, and wax.

claims.text: Longer cotton staples are prized for fine clothing, while shorter fibres go into carpets or blankets.

quotes.quote: Longer staple lengths are highly prized and used for fine clothing, while the shorter fibres are used in carpets or blankets.

claims.text: Down To Earth reports that before the industrial era only two natural dyes, indigo and madder, ensured permanent colour on cotton, a cellulose fibre.

quotes.quote: Before the industrial era, only natural dyes were used. It was found that for cotton, which is a cellulose fibre, only two dyes -- indigo and madder -- ensured permanence of colour.

claims.text: A mordant fixes the dye molecule to the fibre and changes the hue, intensity and fastness of the result.

quotes.quote: A mordant is used in order to fix the dye molecule to the cotton fiber, which also influences the hue, intensity, and colorfastness of the end result.
Mordants are chemicals that react with dyes to change their shade and make them fast.
a mordant, a chemical that increases the interaction between dye and fibre

claims.text: Mordant dyes form complexes with metal mordants, and most give different shades or colours with different mordants.

quotes.quote: This classical definition of mordant dyes has been extended to cover all those dyes which are capable of forming complex with the metal mordant. Most of these dyes yield different shades or colors with different mordants with different hue and tone.

claims.text: With a red dye such as madder or chay root, an alum mordant gives red and an iron mordant gives black.

quotes.quote: Iron acetate would result in a black colour and alum would make it red.
The chay reacts with the alum mordant to produce red, and with the iron mordant to produce black.

claims.text: Alum and iron mordants were accepted for improving colour fastness and broadening the colour range of natural dyes.

quotes.quote: For example, alum, iron mordant were accepted for their improved fastness properties and broadening the color range.

claims.text: Untreated cotton could not absorb madder, so the cloth was first dipped in a tannin solution and then mordanted so the dye could bond and remain insoluble.

quotes.quote: As cotton in its natural state could not absorb madder, it had to be treated to enable the dye to bond with the fibre and remain insoluble. The first stage of the treatment involves dipping the cloth in tannic solution after which mordants would be applied.

claims.text: Myrobalan, or harde, a strong tannin from the fruit of the chebulic myrobalan tree, has traditionally been used as a mordant in India.

quotes.quote: Myrobalan (Harde), a strong tannin from the fruit of Chebulic Myrobalan, a flowering evergreen tree, has traditionally been used as a mordant in India

claims.text: The Met's red Fustat fragment was block-printed with a paste of alum mordant, which fixes the red dye to the cotton only where it was applied.

quotes.quote: The red printed fabric was block printed with a paste of the mordant alum, which fixes the red dye to the cotton fiber, but only in the areas where it was applied

claims.text: On one Fustat print, an iron acetate paste of fermented scrap iron combined with myrobalan tannin to create a corrosive dye that caused fibre loss.

quotes.quote: The darker shade of purple at the center of the leaves was block printed with a paste of iron acetate made of fermented scrap iron, which together with the myrobalan tannin created the corrosive dye that caused fiber loss.

claims.text: Kalamkari black was made by mixing jaggery and iron filings with water.

quotes.quote: black was made by mixing jaggery and iron filings with water

claims.text: Red dyes traditionally used in India, madder-family plants that include al, Indian madder and chay root, are chemically different from each other and from Middle Eastern and European dyer's madder.

quotes.quote: Traditionally, the red dye sourced and used in India has been madder from the Rubiaceae botanical family, growing in different locales.
These plants include some of the following varieties: Indian mulberry (Morinda citrifolia L.), also known as Al; Indian madder or munjeet (Rubia cordifolia); and chay root (Oldenlandia umbellata L.)
These dyes are all chemically different from each other and from the more well-known dyer's madder (Rubia tinctorum L.), which is Middle Eastern and European in origin.

claims.text: Indian madder contains high amounts of alizarin, the main compound responsible for red in most natural dyes.

quotes.quote: Indian madder is a cultivated species of madder that contains high amounts of alizarin, which is the main compound responsible for producing red in most natural dyes.

claims.text: In a preliminary study the Met called inconclusive, liquid chromatography of the red dye on five Indian block prints found al on four and dyer's madder on one.

quotes.quote: analyzed the red dye on five Indian block prints from The Met collection
using a high-performance liquid chromatography-photodiode array detector, and the results demonstrated that Al (Morinda citrifolia L.) was used on four textiles
Dyer's madder (Rubia tinctorum L.) was found on one textile with a very saturated red
This preliminary study is inconclusive due to the small number of textiles analyzed

claims.text: Finding al on the Fustat prints was expected because the al shrub grew in Gujarat.

quotes.quote: This result was expected, as the Al shrub grew in Gujarat

claims.text: A Met article on two fragments in an exhibition on view through January 2017 reports that most Indian artisans often use synthetic alizarin and that chay root has been discontinued.

quotes.quote: In India today, most artisans often use synthetic alizarin-an orange or red crystalline compound-though a discerning customer sometimes requests both Al and munjeet. Chay root has been discontinued and the knowledge of its application seems to be lost.
Jerusalem 1000-1400: Every People Under Heaven, on view through January 8, 2017

claims.text: In pre-industrial India, cloth was mordanted in heated soft water, preferably with alum, then dyed in a separate vat holding crushed madder wrapped in cotton cloth.

quotes.quote: In pre-industrial India, soft water was first heated without bringing it to a boil before adding the cloth and salt- or oil-based mordants, preferably alum, to the water.
A dyebath was then prepared by wrapping the crushed madder in cotton cloth and placing it in a separate vat of water, followed by the mordanted cloth.

claims.text: Because alizarin has low solubility in water, wrapping the madder let the red disperse slowly so the bath coloured evenly and the cloth dyed uniformly.

quotes.quote: Since alizarin has low solubility in water, this method allowed the red colour to disperse through the water slowly, so that the bath was evenly coloured and the cloth dyed uniformly.

claims.text: Impart lists indigo blue, blacks from myrobalan and acacia bark, and reds from madder, chay root, aal and lac insects as the longest-lasting Indian dyes.

quotes.quote: Shades of blue made from indigo, black from haritaki (black myrobalan) and khair (acacia bark), and a range of reds, lilac and burgundy made from manjistha (madder), chay root, aal (Indian mulberry) and lac insects were the longest-lasting dyes

claims.text: Indian yellow dyes come mainly from turmeric root and to a lesser extent from safflower, palash flowers and pomegranate rind.

quotes.quote: Yellow dyes are made mainly from haldi (turmeric root) and to a lesser extent kusumba (safflower), palash (Parrot tree) flowers and pomegranate rind.

claims.text: Natural yellow dyes such as turmeric are relatively short-lived compared with blue or red and fade after several washes and prolonged exposure to light.

quotes.quote: However, natural yellow dyes are relatively short-lived compared to blue or red, as are mixed dyes that use a yellow element, such as greens and oranges.
Like all natural yellow dyes, turmeric is not durable and fades after several washes and prolonged exposure to light.

claims.text: When calico is dyed with turmeric, pomegranate rind and alum are added to brighten the yellow and extend its life.

quotes.quote: When dyeing calico cloth, pomegranate rind and alum are added to brighten the yellow colour and extend its life.

claims.text: Yellow dyed over indigo blue gives green, and turmeric over red gives orange, though the fugitive yellow eventually fades.

quotes.quote: Dyed blue or red cloth is also overdyed with turmeric to obtain shades of green or orange. However, since turmeric is a fugitive dye, the yellow component of the colour eventually fades
Once the wax has been removed, yellow dye can be applied directly over top of the blue areas to produce green.

claims.text: Indigo dye is extracted from Indigofera tinctoria, a plant native to South Asia, and was historically prized because usable blue pigments are rare in nature.

quotes.quote: A natural dye extracted from the Indigofera tinctoria plant native to South Asia
Due to the rarity of usable blue pigments in nature, indigo has historically been a prized good

claims.text: To make indigo, leaves are soaked and churned until they froth blue, the sediment is left to settle, and the blue paste is filtered, pressed into cakes and dried.

quotes.quote: Leaves are harvested before the flowers of the plant bloom and then soaked in water and churned until they release a navy blue froth.
The water and fine sediment at the bottom of the tank are allowed to settle for a day, after which the liquid is separated from the sediment.
This deep blue paste is filtered for dirt and other impurities, pressed into cakes and dried for a few days, after which the indigo is ready to be used as a dye.

claims.text: Indigo plants hold colourless indican, which the enzyme beta-glucosidase turns into colourless indoxyl that oxidises in air to indigo dye.

quotes.quote: which transforms indican (no color) to indoxyl (no color) and produces indigo dye via oxidation (when exposed to air)
Indigo can be extracted from indigo dye-containing plants with water and is processed by intrinsic enzymatic reactions carried out by β-glucosidase in chloroplasts

claims.text: Oxidising extracted indigo by aeration, then heating and air-drying it, is the extraction method popular in India.

quotes.quote: The extracted indigo dye is oxidized by aeration, heated, and air dried or used to make a paste with lime hydrate (Ca(OH)2). The former method is popular in India.

claims.text: Indigo is insoluble in water, so it is reduced to a soluble colourless leuco form that enters the fibre and reoxidises to insoluble blue in air.

quotes.quote: They are insoluble in their colored form, however can undergo reduction into soluble colorless (leuco) form which has an affinity for fibre or textile to be dyed.

Although indigo is not soluble in water, leucoindigo is soluble in water. Therefore, leucoindigo penetrates textiles dipped in indigo fermentation fluid, followed by a brief exposure to air to oxidize leucoindigo
Then, when the fabric is exposed to air, the dye oxidizes to the insoluble blue form, adhering to the fibers permanently.
The fabric would first be dipped into a prepared dye vat and then exposed to air, so that the indigo white could revert into insoluble indigo blue and be bonded to the cotton fibre.

claims.text: Only three natural dyes are vat dyes: indigo, woad and Tyrian purple.

quotes.quote: Only three natural dyes belong to vat dyes: indigo, woad and tyrian purple.

claims.text: Traditional indigo vats reduce the dye by fermentation, carried out by naturally occurring microbes under alkaline, anaerobic conditions.

quotes.quote: Indigo fermentation, which depends on the indigo-reducing action of microorganisms, has traditionally been performed to dye textiles blue in Asia as well as in Europe.
This fermentation process is carried out by naturally occurring microbial communities and occurs under alkaline, anaerobic conditions.
On oxidisation, indigo white is converted into granules of indigo blue which has then to be reduced through fermentation into soluble indigo white, before dyeing can begin.

claims.text: Indigo fermentation has been replaced by chemical reduction with sodium dithionite, whose environmentally unfavourable products make dye waste hard to dispose of.

quotes.quote: Therefore, the fermentation procedure has been replaced with chemical reduction using sodium dithionite (Na2S2O2). However, the addition of Na2S2O2 produces environmentally unfavorable products, which leads problems in the disposal of the dye waste

claims.text: Down To Earth reports that rapid oxidation kept indigo out of block printing, and that in India indigo was usually the last colour applied, to keep unwanted colour from the rest of the fabric.

quotes.quote: As oxidisation is very rapid indigo could not be used in block-printing
In India, indigo was usually the last colour to be applied to prevent unwanted colour from permeating into the rest of the fabric.

claims.text: Fourteenth-century Gujarati prints from Fustat and some eighteenth-century examples show that indigo was sometimes used for printing, although the method is unclear.

quotes.quote: Fragments of fourteenth-century block-printed cloth from Gujarat found in Fustat, Egypt, as well as some later examples from the eighteenth century show that indigo was sometimes used for printing, although the method is unclear.

claims.text: Indian resists against indigo were made of gum and mud or of wax, and the southern centres preferred wax applied in a cold process.

quotes.quote: The fabric itself would be protected by an impermeable substance called the resist which was made in various combinations of gum and mud or from wax. The preferred medium in the southern centres was wax and a cold process was used.

claims.text: A Met article on two fragments in an exhibition on view through January 2017 names dabu, a mud paste whose cracks leave characteristic lines, the most common resist used for indigo.

quotes.quote: The most common resist used for indigo today is a mud paste called Dabu, which often displays the characteristic "crack" lines where the dye penetrated the cracks in the resist
Jerusalem 1000-1400: Every People Under Heaven, on view through January 8, 2017

claims.text: The dabu resist paste is made of chuna (calcium hydroxide), beedan (pounded wheat chaff), mud from the local riverbed and gond (gum), sieved until fine.

quotes.quote: a paste prepared with chuna (calcium hydroxide), beedan (pounded wheat chaff), locally-sourced mud from local riverbed and gond (gum) is sieved until it becomes fine

claims.text: Dabu, a mud-resist printing technique of Rajasthan and Gujarat, takes its name from the Hindi word dabana, meaning to press.

quotes.quote: A mud-resist printing technique practised in Rajasthan and Gujarat, dabu gets its name from the Hindi word dabana which means "to press".

claims.text: Dabu's roots in India are traced to the village of Akora in Rajasthan, where it is still practised and the block printers are known as chippas.

quotes.quote: Its roots in India have been traced to the village Akora, Rajasthan, where it is still actively practised and the block-printers are known as chippas.

claims.text: A Met article describes the current preparation of cotton for block prints like the Fustat fragments as repeated soaking in camel dung, castor oil, soda ash and water, trampling, beating and sun bleaching.

quotes.quote: The first steps of the current production process involved in the creation of the block-printed textiles require long and laborious cleaning and bleaching of the cotton fabric to remove impurities and prepare the fiber to receive the dye

The fabric is immersed in a solution of camel dung, castor oil, soda ash, and water, and then subjected to trampling and beating until a soap-like solution is formed (fig. 4). This treatment is repeated several times, interspersed with laying in the sun to be bleached by oxidation.

claims.text: Beeswax was traditionally the batik resist, but paraffin wax has become the most popular resist over time.

quotes.quote: Beeswax was traditionally used as a resist, but there were local variations as well
Over time, however, paraffin wax has become the most popular resist

claims.text: Impart states that the Kutch batik resist was a paste of hot oil extracted from the seeds of the local pilu tree.

quotes.quote: in the Kutch region of Gujarat, for example, the resist was a paste made of hot oil extracted from the seeds of the local pilu tree

claims.text: Judy Frater writes that Khatri artisans originally used a natural wax laboriously extracted from the fruit of the pilu tree, Salvadora persica.

quotes.quote: Originally, Khatri artisans used a natural wax laboriously extracted from the fruit of the pilu tree (Salvadora persica).

claims.text: Wax resist required cold-water dyes, so indigo and kaiyu mud were the only two natural dyes Kutch artisans used with batik.

quotes.quote: The limitation was that wax required cold-water dyes. Indigo and kaiyu mud were the only cold-water natural dyes; thus, these were the only two natural dyes used with batik.

claims.text: In batik, cloth is dyed in cold water from lighter to darker shades with more areas reserved each time, then boiled so the wax melts away.

quotes.quote: Once the resist is applied, the cloth is dyed in cold water - going from lighter to darker shades - with the process being repeated and more areas being reserved and dyed as needed.
After the required design and colours are achieved, the cloth is boiled in hot water to allow the wax to melt away.

claims.text: Paraffin wax gives finished batik its distinctively veined appearance, as dyes seep into cracks in the wax.

quotes.quote: giving finished batik textiles their distinctively veined appearance as the dyes often seep into the cracks in the wax

claims.text: In India, Bengal, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh are known for batik-printed textiles, with smaller-scale practice elsewhere.

quotes.quote: In India, the states of Bengal, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh are known for batik-printed textiles, although the technique is also practised on a smaller scale in other parts of the country

claims.text: The word batik derives from the Malay titik, a dot, and the Javanese amba, to write, and now denotes wax-resist dyeing worldwide.

quotes.quote: the word batik derives from titik, the Malay word for dot or point and the Javanese word amba, which means "to write." Though Indonesian in its origin, the term has come to be associated with wax-based resist dyeing techniques practiced around the world.

claims.text: In bandhani, tiny sections of cloth are pinched by hand or raised with a metal ring and bound with strong thread before dyeing, and untying reveals small dots of colour surrounded by lighter undyed rings.

quotes.quote: tiny sections of cloth are pinched by hand, or raised with a metal ring, and bound with a strong thread
Once the threads are untied, small dots of colour surrounded by lighter undyed rings are revealed.
Bandhani is a resist-dyeing technique in which small portions of fabric are pinched and tied tightly before the fabric is dyed, resulting in dotted patterns.

claims.text: Bandhani designs were traditionally printed with carved wooden blocks coated with geru, though Impart noted in 2022 that most dyers apply the geru with plastic stencils.

quotes.quote: The design is then printed onto one face of the cloth using specially carved wooden blocks coated with geru. While the blocks are the traditional printing tools, most dyers today apply the geru with stencils made of plastic Farma paper.
First published: 21 April 2022

claims.text: Bandhani takes its name from the Sanskrit baandh, to tie, and is identified by light circular or square repeating motifs on a dark ground.

quotes.quote: Bandhani in its many variations is identified by light circular or square-shaped repeating motifs on a dark ground. It derives its name from the Sanskrit word baandh, meaning "to tie,"

claims.text: Bandhani patterns with numerous small, closely spaced dots are preferred to those with fewer, widely spaced or irregular dots.

quotes.quote: patterns with numerous small and closely spaced dots are preferred to those with fewer, widely spaced or irregular dots

claims.text: In Rajasthan the colours of bandhani came to signal the wearer's community, social position, occupation and marital status.

quotes.quote: with the colours standing as social designators of community, social position, occupation and marital status of the person wearing it

claims.text: Impart in 2022 listed Mandvi, Bhuj, Jamnagar, Porbandar and Rajkot in Gujarat and Udaipur, Jaipur, Ajmer and Bikaner in Rajasthan among major bandhani centres, and a GI journal places Bhuj and Mandvi in Kutch.

quotes.quote: Major centres for bandhani textile production include Mandvi, Bhuj, Jamnagar, Porbandar and Rajkot in Gujarat and Udaipur, Jaipur, Ajmer and Bikaner in Rajasthan.
First published: 21 April 2022
It is one of the most important crafts of Kutch which gives whole or part-time employment to 4,000 persons particularly at Bhuj, Mandvi, Anjar, Mundra and Naliya

claims.text: The skill and time bandhani demands have opened a gap between demand and supply, fuelling printed imitations that have effectively replaced tie-resist dyeing in sungadi textiles.

quotes.quote: the high level of skill coupled with the time-consuming nature of the work has given rise to a disparity in demand and supply

This has led to the growth of printed imitation bandhani designs, which has adversely affected variations such as sungadi textiles to the point of effectively substituting tie-resist dyeing techniques altogether.

claims.text: Sungadi, a close variation of bandhani in Tamil Nadu, is practised by Saurashtrian artisans who migrated to Madurai in the seventeenth century.

quotes.quote: Sungadi, a very similar variation of bandhani found in Tamil Nadu, is practised by Saurashtrian artisans who migrated to Madurai in the seventeenth century at the behest of the local ruler.

claims.text: Unlike bandhani, which reserves small sections, leheriya wrap-resist rolls up the whole cloth and ties it at intervals, so the untied segments take the dye.

quotes.quote: Unlike bandhani, where small sections of the textile are reserved and dyed, the wrap-resist technique of leheriya involves rolling up the entire material and tying it at intervals according to a pattern. The untied segments of the fabric receive the dyes, while the resist segments emerge undyed.

claims.text: Because the dye must penetrate layers of tightly rolled fabric, leheriya demands muslin or fine silks as its base.

quotes.quote: Because the dye needs to penetrate through layers of tightly rolled fabric, the technique demands the use of muslin or fine silks as its base material.

claims.text: Leheriya uses fugitive kuccha dyes so that excess dye discharges easily, leaving clean lines in the pattern.

quotes.quote: Fugitive dyes, also known as kuccha dyes, are used in leheriya, so that the excessive dye may be easily discharged, leaving clean lines in the pattern.

claims.text: Leheriya takes its name from the Sanskrit lahara, wave, and its designs evoke the monsoon and the wind's patterns on desert sand.

quotes.quote: Leheriya derives its name from the Sanskrit word lahara, meaning "wave," and refers to the inspirations behind the designs: the monsoon season - a time of celebration in the state - as well as the patterns created by the wind on the desert sand.

claims.text: Impart in 2022 named the cities of Jodhpur and Jaipur the two main centres of leheriya textiles.

quotes.quote: The cities of Jodhpur and Jaipur are the two main centres of leheriya textiles
First published: 21 April 2022

claims.text: In chintz making, alum and iron mordants are applied with a kalam, a bamboo pen, and the cotton is then dyed in a bath of chay root.

quotes.quote: Then, alum and iron mordants are applied to the cloth using a kalam (a bamboo pen).
The cotton is then submerged in a dye bath of chay root, a natural red dye from the Coromandel Coast.

claims.text: After the reds, chintz is covered in beeswax except where blue is wanted, then dipped into indigo, the wax resisting the dye.

quotes.quote: Once all the desired red shades have been acheived, the whole cloth is covered in beeswax excepting those areas that are to be dyed blue. Then the cloth is dipped into an indigo dye bath. The wax resists the dye, and protects the rest of the cloth.

claims.text: Chintz is made by a combination of mordant dyeing and resist dyeing of cotton, with pre-treatment, washing and bleaching between colours.

quotes.quote: Chintz is made by a combination of mordant and resist-dyeing cotton.
Making chintz involves many additional stages in which the cloth is pre-treated, washed and bleached in between each colour.

claims.text: In the Beaulieu manuscript's chintz process the cloth is dunged and bleached four times; the manuscript recommended kid-dung, which the Winterthur reconstruction replaced with wheat bran and chalk.

quotes.quote: The cloth will undergo four dungings and bleachings in all during the process of chintz making.

In the absence of kid-dung, which was recommended by the Beaulieu manuscript for dunging, a modern version of soaking cloth in a mixture of wheat bran and chalk (calcium carbonate) mixed with warm water, was adopted.

claims.text: In a reconstruction of the Beaulieu manuscript, the first madder bath was heated but kept under 60°C for 2 hours.

quotes.quote: It was immersed in a bath made of powdered madder root and water, and brought up to heat in the bath, with temperature maintained under 60°C, for 2 hours.

claims.text: Chintz makers of the Coromandel Coast were particularly admired for the brilliance of their colours and the delicacy of their designs.

quotes.quote: Chintz makers from the Coromandel Coast were particularly admired for the brilliance of their colours and the delicacy of their designs.

claims.text: The Tree of Life, often with deep red flowers, was a popular chintz motif among British consumers, and also recurs on Indian carpets.

quotes.quote: A popular motif among British consumers was the Tree of Life, which was frequently depicted with deep red flowers characteristic of Indian chintz.
Carpets typically feature recurring motifs, including palmettes, geometrical shapes, flowers, the tree of life and occasionally, animals.

claims.text: Chintz, a glazed plain-weave cotton printed with floral and geometric patterns, takes its name from the Hindi chint, meaning spotted.

quotes.quote: A glazed cotton fabric with a plain or tabby weave, typically printed with floral and geometric patterns
The word derives from the Hindi word chint, meaning "spotted."

claims.text: Kalamkari has twenty-three steps, including treating cotton with cow dung and bleach and soaking it in buffalo milk and myrobalan so it retains the dyes.

quotes.quote: Kalamkari consists of twenty-three steps including treating the fabric by bleaching it and then softening it

Commonly, cotton is used which is then treated with a solution of cow dung and bleach casting the fabric in an off-white colour. This is followed by the immersion of fabric in a mixture of buffalo milk and myrobalans so that it absorbs and retains the colour of dyes and paints without smudging.

claims.text: Kalamkari emerged across the Coromandel coast with Andhra Pradesh its focal centre around Srikalahasti, in Chittoor district, and other centres at Machilipatnam, headquarters of Krishna district, and Madurai.

quotes.quote: A textile tradition where cotton textiles are traditionally hand-painted with pictorial narratives through a bamboo pen known as kalam, kalamkari emerged across the Coromandel coast in southern India and the state of Andhra Pradesh has long been considered its focal centre.
Concentrated largely around the town of Srikalahasti, kalamkari's other major centres of production include Machilipatnam (formerly Masulipatnam) and Madurai.
Srikalahasti, Chitoor, District, Andhra Pradesh
Machilipatnam, the head quarter of Krishna district in coastal Andhra Pradesh

claims.text: Down To Earth reported that Masulipatnam printed its mordant uniformly with blocks, while Kalahasti relied entirely on drawing with the pen.

quotes.quote: In Masulipatnam, mordant is uniformly printed with a block.
a major difference is that in Kalahasti there is total reliance on the pen

claims.text: The term kalamkari derives from the tools artisans used to apply resist and mordant; in medieval India this was a brush-like instrument called the kalam.

quotes.quote: The term kalamkari is derived from the tools used by the artisans to apply resist and mordant. In medieval India a brush-like instrument called the kalam was used.

claims.text: Painted kalamkari textiles depicted scenes from the Puranas and epics such as the Mahabharata and Ramayana, the Ramayana being notably popular.

quotes.quote: Themes depicted in the textile included scenes from Puranas and epics such as Mahabharata and Ramayana, with the latter enjoying a notable popularity.

claims.text: Zari is a gold or silver thread used in brocade and zardosi designs, its name from the Persian zar, meaning gold.

quotes.quote: A gold or silver thread used in brocade and zardosi designs. It is typically used to decorate silk saris, ghaghras or border designs. From the Persian word zar, meaning 'gold'.

claims.text: Embroidery with zari, or gold thread, was practised through most of South Asian history in major weaving centres such as Varanasi and Kanchipuram.

quotes.quote: embroidery using zari, or gold thread, practised through most of South Asian history in major weaving centres such as Varanasi and Kanchipuram

claims.text: Sozni embroidery from Kashmir uses dense needlework for all-over floral designs, while kasuti from Karnataka uses a counting-thread technique for angular designs.

quotes.quote: The dense needlework used for the all-over floral designs of sozni embroidery from Kashmir, and the counting-thread technique of angular, carefully proportioned kasuti designs from Karnataka are examples of such ornate textiles.

claims.text: Banjara embroidery on red-dyed cotton is embellished with bells, beads, cowries, shisha, metal bits, coins and tassels.

quotes.quote: embellished by a variety of visually distinct materials such as bells, beads, cowries, shisha, metal bits, coins and tassels are integrated into the embroidery patterns, often covering the entirety of the base fabric, which is typically red-dyed cotton
the highly varied embroidery of the nomadic Banjara community, who add coins, sequins and cowrie shells to their colourful designs

claims.text: In Banjara embroidery shishas appear frequently for their reflectiveness, while cowrie shells and coins add symbolic value.

lede.text: Textile crafts pattern cloth with dye in printing and tie-resist work, where mordants fix madder reds and resists of mud, gum, wax or tied thread hold back indigo; with thread and cut cloth added by needle in embroidery and applique; and with structure in carpets of knotted wool, flat-woven dhurries and felted namdas.

They are practised from the resist-dyeing centres of Gujarat and Rajasthan and the Coromandel coast, where kalamkari emerged, to Kashmir, a hub of carpet making, by communities that include the Khatri and Chippa block printers and the nomadic Banjara.

Red runs through the category: an alum mordant turns madder or chay root red, phulkari's khaddar is traditionally dyed red with plant dyes, Banjara embroidery is typically set on red-dyed cotton, and Mughal carpets were distinguished by brighter, primarily red colours.

Their history runs from madder-dyed cotton at Mohenjo-daro and block prints found at Fustat and ascribed to Gujarat to the early eighteenth-century bans by which Britain and France shielded their industries from Indian chintzes and muslins.

sentences.text: Ornamentation is a key aspect of craftsmanship in the Indian subcontinent and is perhaps most striking in its textile crafts.
Indian dyes were coveted for their vibrancy and for carefully guarded dyeing processes, which often involved mordants that fixed the colour to the fabric and made it uniquely durable.

Block printing stamps cotton or silk with dye-soaked, hand-carved wooden blocks, a technique central to a variety of Indian printing traditions, and the Khatris and Chippas have practised it continuously since at least the sixteenth century.
The specialised skills of embroidery, sometimes months of work on one garment, often make luxury textiles, and techniques such as sozni and beetle wing embroidery have resisted mechanisation.
Applique traditions such as pipili, tharu, kantha and khatwa repurpose fabric from old or damaged garments into everyday items such as bags and kowdhi quilts.
Kantha, from the Sanskrit kontha, rags, is a household embroidery of women in West Bengal and Bangladesh, applied on quilts, bags and other textiles of reused fabric.
Rajasthan and neighbouring Gujarat share a long-established tradition of resist-dyed textiles, particularly bandhani, a name from the Sanskrit baandh, to tie.
Notable Indian carpets and rugs include gabba, kaleen, galeecha and dhurrie, and dhurries differ from carpets in their flat weave, relative lightness and often reversible designs.
A Mehrgarh thread of approximately 5500 BCE is the earliest evidence of cotton cultivation, and cotton cloth was made in India as early as 5000 BCE.
Madder-dyed cotton from Mohenjo-daro of the second millennium BCE is the earliest evidence of Indian textile dyes, and the Atharvaveda holds the earliest literary mention of indigo.

Sources differ on whether the Indian block prints found at Fustat were collected or excavated, and fragments of the group, ascribed to Gujarat, are dated variously from the 13th to 14th century to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

Chintz and calico were traded across the Indian Ocean as far back as the fifteenth century, and in the early eighteenth century Britain and France banned imported cotton to protect their industries from Indian chintzes and muslins.

Embroidery and applique from the subcontinent were mentioned in the first-century CE Periplus of the Erythrean Sea, the oldest extant Indian applique dates to the twelfth century at Pipili, and by the eighteenth century ari work had reached Europe.

Bandhani was originally practised by the Khatri community in Sindh, dabu has been traced to an eighth-century fabric specimen from Central Asia, and Indonesian batik techniques were taught at Shantiniketan after Tagore's 1927 visit to Java and Bali.

Hand-knotted carpets in India date to about 985 CE by one account, though Akbar is widely credited with introducing them, and under Jahangir, Akhund Rahmuna spread carpet making among Kashmiri weavers.
Natural dyes were largely replaced by European synthetic dyes by the late nineteenth century, and by 1914 natural indigo made up only four percent of global indigo use.

Between the eleventh and nineteenth centuries Indian cloth held the largest share of the global cotton trade, Gujarati cottons going mostly to African and Persian Gulf ports and Indonesia and southern cottons chiefly to Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines.
As many as forty-six Indian carpets were exported to England in 1619, and Impart in 2022 described the Indian carpet industry as primarily export-oriented.
By the mid nineteenth century Indian consumers largely bought cheaper British-made chintz, and from the 1950s traditional clients came to prefer cheaper mass-produced textiles over handcraft.
Printed imitations of bandhani have effectively replaced tie-resist dyeing in sungadi textiles, and handmade applique faces strong competition from cheaper mass-produced textiles.
Srikalahasti kalamkari registered a geographical indication in 2006, chikankari received GI status in 2008 and Machilipatnam kalamkari in 2009.

Registered GIs include embroideries such as Kasuti, Phulkari, Kutch Embroidery and Toda Embroidery, hand block prints such as Sanganeri, Bagru and Kutch Ajrakh, and carpets of Bhadohi, Kashmir and Gwalior.

Other textile GIs include Madurai Sungudi, Jamnagari and Kutch Bandhani, Mata ni Pachhedi, Narasapur Crochet Lace Products, Lahauli Knitted Socks & Gloves, Patchwork of Rampur, Ujjain Batik Print and Santiniketan Batik Textile.
India Water Portal, writing after a High Court directive of May 2015, reported that the Sanganer printing cluster employs almost 10,000 people directly and indirectly.
Each export market for Indian dyed cottons had its own layout, motifs and colour, which makers followed rigidly to ensure sales.

In Indian societies each caste or community wore a specific dress, with colour and pattern marking age, social status and occasion, and in Rajasthan bandhani colours came to signal community, occupation and marital status.
Bandhani prizes numerous small, closely spaced dots, while leheriya, named from the Sanskrit lahara, wave, evokes the monsoon and the wind's patterns on desert sand.
Coromandel chintz makers were admired for the brilliance of their colours and the delicacy of their designs, and the Tree of Life recurs on chintz and on Indian carpets.
Mughal-era carpets differed from Persian ones in their brighter colours, primarily red, and their fine knotting of about 4424 knots per square inch.
The woven patterns of dhurries are based originally on floor decorations such as rangoli and kolam.

Embroidery ranges from the dense floral sozni of Kashmir and the counted-thread kasuti of Karnataka to shisha, or mirror-work, set into Banjara work and into the Ahir embroidery of the Kutch tradition.
Paraffin wax gives finished batik its distinctively veined appearance as dyes seep into cracks in the wax.

Most Indian cotton exports left from ports on the western and eastern coasts serving Gujarat, Kerala, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, and some of the major mordanting centres were in Gujarat and at Masulipatnam, Kalahasti, Pulicat and the Tanjore region on the Coromandel coast.

Impart in 2022 listed Mandvi, Bhuj, Jamnagar, Porbandar and Rajkot in Gujarat and Udaipur, Jaipur, Ajmer and Bikaner in Rajasthan among major bandhani centres, and Jodhpur and Jaipur as the two main leheriya centres.

Kalamkari emerged across the Coromandel coast with Andhra Pradesh its focal centre around Srikalahasti and other centres at Machilipatnam and Madurai, and Bengal, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh are known for batik-printed textiles.

Woodblock carving has traditionally been carried out in Gujarat and Rajasthan, with Jaipur Rajasthan's primary block-making centre, and by the nineteenth century Jaipur had also emerged as the main centre for zari and badla, alongside Lucknow and Surat.
Kutch, an arid district of Gujarat lying between Sindh and mainland Gujarat, historically grew indigo, as did Sindh.
The carpet trade raised northern centres such as Bhadohi, Mirzapur, Amritsar and Panipat; historic centres lay mostly in the north and west, contemporary ones also in the south and north-east.

Dhurries came to replace carpets in warmer regions and months, while namdas, used in Kashmir as warm mattresses and floor coverings, have prominent centres at Tonk in Rajasthan and Srinagar in Kashmir.
Impart in 2022 named Hoshiarpur, Jodhpur, Varanasi, Warangal, Salem, Panipat, Belgaum and Pune as the chief dhurrie centres.

A printed motif may need several blocks, such as a rekh for the outline, a datta to fill it and a gadh for the background, which requires block maker and printer to know how every block fits the design, and air passages called pavansar keep blocks from clinging to the fabric.

A Met article describes the current preparation of cotton for block prints like the Fustat fragments as repeated soaking in camel dung, castor oil, soda ash and water with sun bleaching, and Gujarat stamped mordants with wooden blocks while the Coromandel coast preferred transfer and the brush or pen.
Chintz combines mordant and resist dyeing: alum and iron mordants are applied with a kalam, the cloth is dyed in chay root, then waxed except where blue is wanted and dipped in indigo.

Resists against indigo were made of gum and mud or of wax, and a Met article names the mud paste dabu the most common, while bandhani binds tiny sections of cloth with thread before dyeing and leheriya rolls up and ties the whole cloth.
Sources differ on indigo in block printing: Down To Earth says rapid oxidation kept it out, while Impart says Fustat prints show indigo was sometimes used for printing by an unclear method.
Chikankari employs at least thirty stitches in three groups, ari embroidery makes chain stitch with a hooked needle, and phulkari and kantha are worked in running stitch.

Indian carpets, most commonly woven on roller-beam looms, use the asymmetrical Persian knot in most traditions by one account and exclusively by another, while dhurries are weft-faced weaves on horizontal pit looms and namdas are layered wool pressed together.
Mata ni pachedi uses woodblocks, usually for the borders, and a bamboo kalam for many drawings and motifs, on cloth first treated with a harda solution.

Cotton contains 88-96% pure alpha cellulose; Down To Earth reports that before the industrial era only indigo and madder ensured permanent colour on it, while Impart lists myrobalan and acacia blacks and lac reds too among the longest-lasting Indian dyes.
A mordant fixes the dye to the fibre and changes its hue, intensity and fastness, and mordant dyes form complexes with metal mordants that give different shades.
With madder or chay root, an alum mordant gives red and an iron mordant gives black, and untreated cotton was first dipped in a tannin solution before mordanting.
Before block printing a mordant is typically added to the dye because many natural dyes do not easily adhere to cloth, while indigo needs no mordant.
Indian madder contains high amounts of alizarin, whose low solubility in water let wrapped madder colour a dyebath slowly and evenly.
Indigo plants hold colourless indican, which the enzyme beta-glucosidase turns into colourless indoxyl that oxidises in air to indigo.

Insoluble indigo is reduced to a soluble colourless form that enters the fibre and reoxidises to blue in air, and sources differ on the traditional method: microbial fermentation in alkaline, anaerobic vats, or a reducing agent such as zinc or ammonia added to a hot bath.
Yellow dyes come mainly from turmeric root and fade with washing and light, though alum and pomegranate rind brighten turmeric yellow, and yellow over indigo gives green.
Cotton is a seed-hair fibre of the genus Gossypium, its longer staples prized for fine clothing and its shorter fibres used in carpets or blankets.
India has the unique distinction of producing all the commercial silks, mulberry, tasar, muga and eri, and silk in the subcontinent is, and historically has been, a luxury good.
Pashmina, combed by hand from the undercoat of Changthangi goats, has fibres twelve to sixteen microns in diameter and is warmer, softer and lighter than sheep wool.
Indian carpets are typically wool knotted on a cotton warp and weft, and rarely, as in Kashmir, silk.

Red dyes traditionally used in India include al, Indian madder and chay root, chemically different from each other and from dyer's madder, and myrobalan, a strong tannin, has traditionally been used as a mordant in India.
Dabu resist paste mixes calcium hydroxide, pounded wheat chaff, mud from the local riverbed and gum, while beeswax was the traditional batik resist and paraffin wax is now the most popular.
Printing blocks of woods such as sheesham, sagwan and rohida are often preferred to metal or terracotta for ease of carving, and teak is preferred because water leaves it undamaged.
Zari is a gold or silver thread, and gota work embellishes textiles with gold or silver trims, though lurex, a synthetic yarn, has almost completely replaced metal gota.
Metallic mordants leave wastewater with residual toxic metal ions, and chemical reduction of indigo with sodium dithionite produces environmentally unfavourable dye waste.

At Sanganer, effluents from printing and dyeing units were released untreated into nallahs that drain into the Dravyawati river, and India Water Portal reports that the health of artisans exposed to polluted waters is at risk.

A Sanganer artisan says that washing fabric in the local nallah water gives it amazing shine, and in India it is common to see fields strewn with lengths of fabric laid out to dry and bask in the sun.
